design_detail: Pooled analysis of individual-participant data from 83 prospective studies in 19 high-income countries, not chosen by systematic search: the cohorts are the three data sources available to the investigators' consortium, namely the 81 Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration (ERFC) cohorts that recorded the amount drunk (of 102 with drinking status), EPIC-CVD (a case-cohort study nested in the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition, 22 of 23 centres) and UK Biobank. The literature search in the Research in context box was for background only. Main analysis restricted to 599,912 current drinkers without known cardiovascular disease (CVD) at baseline; Cox models fitted within each study and pooled by random-effects meta-analysis; hazard ratios (HRs) corrected for regression dilution with 152,640 repeat alcohol assessments from 71,011 participants in 37 studies, so that they refer to long-term average (‘usual’) intake.
can_establish: How all-cause mortality and first cardiovascular events vary with self-reported alcohol intake among current drinkers, mostly aged 40 to 80 and without known CVD, in high-income countries, relative to the lightest current drinkers, with large numbers and a common analysis across 83 cohorts.
cannot_establish: Whether drinking any amount carries more or less risk than not drinking (never and former drinkers were excluded from the main analyses); that alcohol causes the associations (observational data, main models adjusted only for age, sex, smoking status and diabetes, and residual reverse causation from people who cut down because of illness, which the authors acknowledge); the effect of reducing intake within a person; a precise threshold (it is read from category HRs plotted in a figure, with no interval of its own); risks in low- and middle-income countries; or outcomes the cohorts did not generally record (non-fatal liver disease, injuries, psychiatric conditions).

sample.recruitment: Registry/cohort: existing population cohorts pooled by the consortium. ERFC: 81 studies in 19 countries, recruited 1964 to 2008, follow-up to 2013; EPIC-CVD: 22 centres in 10 European countries, recruited 1990 to 2002, follow-up to 2009, case-cohort design (all-cause deaths only from the 13,670-person random subcohort); UK Biobank: England, Scotland and Wales, recruited 2006 to 2010, follow-up to 2016 (Table 1; Methods › Study design, data sources, and participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Required: recorded amount drunk and drinking status (non-drinker or current drinker), age, sex, history of diabetes and smoking status; at least 1 year of follow-up after baseline; no known baseline CVD (coronary heart disease, other heart disease, stroke, transient ischaemic attack, peripheral arterial disease or cardiovascular surgery). Main analyses restricted to current drinkers. For each outcome, studies with fewer than five incident cases were excluded (Methods › Study design, data sources, and participants, 3rd paragraph; Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Current drinkers: mean age 57 (SD 9); 265,910 (44%) women; 128,085 (21%) current smokers; recruitment years 1964 to 2010. Median baseline intake 96 g/week (5th to 95th percentiles 6 to 448); by source, median 87.7 g/week in ERFC, 61.9 in EPIC-CVD and 103.9 in UK Biobank; current smokers 35%, 32% and 10% respectively; history of diabetes 3 to 4% (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1). Ethnicity is mentioned only as differing between never and current drinkers (appendix, not read).
sample.attrition: Median follow-up 7.5 years (5th to 95th percentiles 5.0 to 18.4), 5.4 million person-years. Loss to follow-up is not reported in the main text. Analyses are complete-case; a multiple-imputation analysis for current drinkers with a missing amount is said to give similar results (appendix p 32, not read). The text gives 786,787 participants with sufficient information but not how many were excluded for insufficient information.
sample.selection_effects: Cohorts were those available to the consortium, not found by search, and UK Biobank supplies 54% of the current drinkers (326,372 of 599,912; editors' arithmetic). Participants enter in mid-life as prevalent current drinkers: people who had stopped (including because of illness) are excluded by design, but people who had cut down because of illness stay in the lighter categories, and people harmed by drinking, or who died, before recruitment are not represented. Requiring 1 year of follow-up and no baseline CVD selects healthier participants. The 71,011 with repeat measures (about 12%; editors' arithmetic) were younger, more often men and drank slightly more than the rest, yet supply the correction applied to everyone (Results, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported intake from each cohort's own instrument (self-administered or interviewer-led questionnaires; food-frequency questionnaires or dietary recall), harmonised to grams of pure alcohol per week with 1 UK unit = 8 g (conversion in appendix pp 1 to 2, not read). No biological verification. Long-term average (‘usual’) intake estimated by multilevel regression calibration from repeat surveys (ERFC, UK Biobank) or lifetime-intake measures (EPIC-CVD); regression dilution ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.52), similar to systolic blood pressure (0.52) and lower than HDL cholesterol (0.74) in the same participants (Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Eight predefined baseline categories in g/week: >0 to ≤25 (reference category), >25 to ≤50, >50 to ≤75, >75 to ≤100, >100 to ≤150, >150 to ≤250, >250 to ≤350 and >350. Linear analyses per 100 g/week of usual intake (12.5 UK units). The authors equate 100 g/week with about 5 to 6 standard UK glasses of wine or pints of beer, and the US limit for men (196 g/week) with about 11. Frequency dichotomized at up to 2 versus more than 2 drinking days a week; episodic heavy drinking as 100 g or more per occasion; beverage type wine, beer or spirits (exploratory). Life-expectancy groups: >0 to ≤100 g/week (reference; mean usual 56 g), >100 to ≤200 (123 g), >200 to ≤350 (208 g), >350 (367 g).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking status (current or not) adjusted in all models; smoking amount (pack-years) only in subsets, where it abolished the association of alcohol with lung cancer (appendix p 16, as reported in Results, 4th paragraph). Use of other drugs not measured or not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (intake at baseline, outcomes during follow-up).

comparison.controls: The lightest current drinkers (>0 to ≤25 g/week) for the category analyses (Figures 1 and 2); along the intake gradient within current drinkers for the per-100 g/week HRs (Figure 3, Table 2); drinkers of >0 to ≤100 g/week for life expectancy (Figure 4). Never drinkers and former drinkers were excluded from the main analyses; analyses including them, which reproduce U-shaped curves, are only in the appendix (p 31, not read).
comparison.matching: None. Stratified by sex and study or centre; adjusted for age, smoking status and history of diabetes.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Drinking history before baseline (apart from the EPIC-CVD lifetime measures used for calibration), why people drank at their current level (including having cut down because of illness), and, in the main models, socio-economic position, physical activity, diet, mental health and general health; some cohorts did not record chronic disease other than CVD at baseline (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: All-cause mortality (40,310 deaths, including 11,762 vascular and 15,150 neoplastic); first incident CVD events (39,018): myocardial infarction (MI, 14,539), coronary disease excluding MI (7,990), stroke of all subtypes (12,090), heart failure (2,711), and deaths from other CVD (1,121: dysrhythmia, hypertensive disease, sudden death, aortic aneurysm), as recorded by each cohort; definitions in appendix p 5 (not read). Cancers of the digestive system and lung cancer are reported from the appendix.
outcomes.validity_norms: How deaths and events were ascertained (registries, records, adjudication) is not described in the main text and differs between cohorts; the authors note that outcome misclassification would dilute dose-response associations (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is a higher hazard of death or of a first CVD event. The ‘threshold for lowest risk’ is the intake above which category HRs for all-cause mortality rise in Figure 1 (an image); no formal threshold estimate or interval is given. Years of life lost were modelled by applying age-at-risk-specific HRs for baseline intake categories to US death rates for 2007 to 2010 (CDC WONDER), not observed in the cohorts (Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the main outcomes. 11 counts all-cause mortality, total CVD, MI, coronary disease excluding MI, stroke, heart failure, other CVD deaths and its four components named in the Methods; cancers, stroke subtypes, fatal and non-fatal splits and many subgroup and sensitivity analyses are in the appendix. Interaction tests used a 0.1% significance level and the choice of second-order fractional polynomials a 1% level (Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; outcomes were recorded by the contributing cohorts independently of this analysis.

analysis.effect_sizes: HR per 100 g/week higher usual intake within current drinkers, adjusted for age, smoking and diabetes and stratified by sex and centre: stroke 1.14 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.17); coronary disease excluding MI 1.06 (1.00 to 1.11); heart failure 1.09 (1.03 to 1.15); fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15 to 1.33); fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28); MI 0.94 (0.91 to 0.97) (Abstract; Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3). All-cause mortality: positive and curvilinear, lowest at or below about 100 g/week relative to >0 to ≤25 g/week (Figure 1; category HRs not given as numbers in the text). Table 2, subsets with the covariate measured, per 100 g/week, basic then further adjusted: systolic blood pressure subset, stroke 1.16 (1.11 to 1.22) to 1.10 (1.06 to 1.14), MI 0.95 (0.91 to 0.99) to 0.91 (0.87 to 0.94), coronary excluding MI 1.06 (1.00 to 1.12) to 1.03 (0.97 to 1.10), heart failure 1.11 (1.04 to 1.18) to 1.08 (1.02 to 1.15), other CVD deaths 1.16 (1.06 to 1.27) to 1.14 (1.03 to 1.25); HDL cholesterol subset, stroke 1.16 (1.10 to 1.23) to 1.17 (1.11 to 1.22), MI 0.93 (0.88 to 0.97) to 1.00 (0.96 to 1.04), coronary excluding MI 1.07 (0.98 to 1.17) to 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22), heart failure 1.09 (1.00 to 1.19) to 1.14 (1.01 to 1.27), other CVD deaths 1.22 (1.06 to 1.40) to 1.22 (1.08 to 1.38); body-mass index subset, little change (for example MI 0.95 to 0.94). Heterogeneity I2: stroke 12%, MI 12%, coronary excluding MI 26%, heart failure 4%, other CVD deaths 33%. Life expectancy at age 40 compared with >0 to ≤100 g/week: about 6 months shorter for >100 to ≤200 g/week, 1 to 2 years for >200 to ≤350 and 4 to 5 years for >350 (no intervals in the text); men above 112 g/week 1.6 years shorter (1.3 to 1.8), above 196 g/week 2.7 years (2.4 to 3.1); women above 112 or 98 g/week about 1.3 years (1.1 to 1.5).
analysis.covariates: Main models: age, smoking status (current or not) and history of diabetes, stratified by sex and study or centre; EPIC-CVD case-cohort analysed with Prentice weights. In subsets, usual levels of body-mass index, systolic blood pressure, HDL and LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol and fibrinogen, and baseline pack-years, education, occupation, physical activity, self-rated general health, red meat intake and antihypertensive drug use (Methods › Statistical analysis, 4th paragraph); results for most of these are only in the appendix (pp 15, 30, not read). Blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, other lipids and fibrinogen are potential mediators rather than confounders, as the authors treat them.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is cited. The principal analysis of current drinkers is described as prespecified (Results, 1st paragraph) and the eight intake categories as predefined (Methods › Study design, 3rd paragraph), without a reference to a protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The category-specific HRs for all-cause mortality on which the headline threshold rests appear only in Figure 1 (an image) and appendix p 25, not as numbers in the article, and the threshold is stated only in words. The analyses that include never and former drinkers, and most sensitivity analyses, are summarized as similar or as reproducing earlier findings with the numbers in the appendix (pp 18, 31 to 37). Results modelled on EU death rates are described as similar, data not shown.
analysis.power: Very large: 40,310 deaths and 39,018 first CVD events. Precision is lower for heart failure (2,711 events) and other CVD deaths (1,121), and for the subsets with HDL cholesterol (UK Biobank lipids were not yet available).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 599,912 current drinkers in 83 cohorts, all-cause mortality was lowest in the categories up to about 100 g/week and rose above that, relative to people drinking more than 0 and up to 25 g/week. Higher intake went roughly linearly with more stroke, heart failure, coronary disease other than MI, fatal hypertensive disease and fatal aortic aneurysm, and log-linearly with less MI (HR 0.94 per 100 g/week), an inverse association that disappeared after adjustment for HDL cholesterol (1.00, 0.96 to 1.04). Modelled life expectancy at 40 was lower in heavier-drinking groups, with about 20% of the difference in men attributed to CVD deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the conclusion state that among current drinkers “the threshold for lowest risk of all-cause mortality was about 100 g/week” and that the data support lower guideline limits; the Research in context box calls this the chief implication for policy. Gaps: (1) the threshold is lowest risk among current drinkers only, because the comparison is with the lightest drinkers; the analysis says nothing about drinking up to 100 g/week against not drinking, although a guideline limit is read that way; (2) the discussion says that long-term reduction from 196 to 100 g/week or below was associated with 1 to 2 years longer life expectancy for men, which describes a change within people that the study did not observe: the figure compares different people by baseline intake and is modelled on US death rates; (3) the threshold is read from plotted category HRs, without an interval, and the plotted values are not printed; (4) the main models adjust only for age, sex, smoking status and diabetes, and the authors concede residual reverse causation; (5) the suggestion that HDL-related pathways mediate the lower MI risk is a hypothesis drawn from how the HR changed with adjustment. The abstract does restrict its conclusion to current drinkers in high-income countries, and the discussion lists the main limitations and calls for randomized trials.

timeline.event: Ronksley et al. meta-analysis of alcohol and cardiovascular outcomes, cited among the earlier literature on risk thresholds (carded in this round by another reader).
Holmes et al. Mendelian randomization analysis, cited by the authors as concordant with their cardiovascular findings (carded in this round by another reader).
Stockwell et al. meta-analysis of 87 cohorts referenced to abstainers (card sc_stockwell_2016, this round): a different comparison, which Wood et al. do not cite.
This analysis, with a linked Lancet comment by Connor and Hall, ‘Thresholds for safer alcohol use might need lowering’ (Lancet 391:1460–1461; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)30545-2; not read).
Correction (Lancet 391:2212; doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31168-1): one author's affiliation corrected; no data changed (read).

Letters titled ‘Risk thresholds for alcohol consumption’ by Astrup, Costanzo and de Gaetano, by Schernhammer and by Thompson (Lancet 392:2165–2167), listed on PubMed as comments on this paper (not read).
Commentary by Xuan in BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine (24:117–118), listed on PubMed (not read).
Zhao et al. update of the abstainer-referenced meta-analysis (card sc_zhao_2023, this round); Wood et al. is not among its included studies.

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication of the threshold within current drinkers was identified in what was read this session, so the status reflects only that reading. The study answers a narrower question than the abstainer-referenced meta-analyses (Stockwell et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2023) and the burden-of-disease and genetic studies carded by other readers, and the numbers are not interchangeable: 100 g/week is about 14 g/day (editors' arithmetic), inside the 1.3 to 25 g/day ‘low-volume’ category of those meta-analyses. The divergence between MI and the other cardiovascular outcomes is the study's most distinctive result, and its linked letters and comment have not been read.

funding.affiliations_note: A consortium paper (Emerging Risk Factors Collaboration/EPIC-CVD/UK Biobank Alcohol Study Group) coordinated from the University of Cambridge, with investigators of the contributing cohorts as authors. The declared ties are to pharmaceutical, device and insurance companies and public funders; none names an alcohol producer. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A long-term randomized trial of moderate drinking against abstention or reduction (the authors cite a proposal for one); failing that, pooled cohorts that record drinking from early adulthood with repeated, biomarker-checked measures and correctly classified never and former drinkers, analysed together with genetic methods able to estimate the shape of the curve at low intake.

domains.note: Main models adjust only for age, smoking status (current or not) and diabetes, stratified by sex and centre. Socio-economic position, physical activity, diet and self-rated health were added only in subsets reported in appendix pages not read; the authors say further adjustment changed little except for the mediators blood pressure and HDL cholesterol. Smoking amount explained the lung-cancer association, which shows residual confounding by smoking at this level of adjustment. Reverse causation from people who had cut down because of illness remains, as the authors say, and some cohorts did not record chronic disease other than CVD.

Single baseline self-report from heterogeneous instruments harmonised at 8 g per UK unit; the regression dilution ratio of 0.50 shows large within-person variation, corrected from the 12% with repeat measures, who differed from the rest. Error is probably non-differential with respect to later outcomes, but under-reporting would mean that 100 g/week reported corresponds to more drunk.

Prevalent current drinkers entering in mid-life: former drinkers removed by design, earlier casualties of drinking absent, survival of at least 1 year and absence of CVD required. Cohorts chosen by availability to the consortium, with UK Biobank 54% of participants.

Changes in drinking and medical treatment during follow-up (for example antihypertensive drugs, adjusted for only in subsets) are not modelled beyond calibrating baseline intake to its long-term average; advice to cut down after diagnoses could attenuate associations.

Complete-case analysis; the number excluded for missing intake or covariates is not reported in the main text; multiple imputation reportedly agreed (appendix p 32, not read). EPIC-CVD deaths come from its random subcohort only.

Death is reliably recorded, so the risk is low for all-cause mortality; ascertainment of CVD subtypes differs across 83 cohorts and is described only in the appendix, and hypertensive disease and aortic aneurysm are fatal events only.

No protocol or registration cited for a principal analysis described as prespecified; the threshold is read from plotted categories rather than estimated; many outcomes, subgroups and sensitivity analyses, most reported only in the appendix; beverage-type and pattern results are labelled exploratory.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The gradient of rising mortality above about 100 g/week among current drinkers is estimated with unusual precision and consistency (83 cohorts, individual data, low heterogeneity, stable in sensitivity analyses), and the current-drinker design avoids the former-drinker problem of abstainer-referenced analyses. Attributing the gradient to alcohol, and above all locating the threshold and interpreting the lower MI risk, requires accepting minimal adjustment and residual reverse causation from illness-related reduction, hence high risk of bias overall. The card may be cited for the shape of the associations of self-reported intake with mortality and with cardiovascular subtypes among current drinkers in high-income countries, for the divergence between MI and other cardiovascular outcomes, and for modelled life-expectancy differences between intake groups. It should not be cited for any comparison of drinking with not drinking, for a causal or ‘safe’ threshold, or for the effect of cutting down.

key_findings.finding: Of 786,787 participants with sufficient information for inclusion, 186,875 reported not drinking at baseline, leaving 599,912 current drinkers (ERFC 247,504; EPIC-CVD 26,036; UK Biobank 326,372). Over 5.4 million person-years (median follow-up 7.5 years) there were 40,310 deaths (11,762 vascular, 15,150 neoplastic) and 39,018 first CVD events (12,090 stroke, 14,539 MI, 7,990 coronary disease excluding MI, 2,711 heart failure, 1,121 other CVD deaths).
key_findings.note: The text gives the non-drinkers as 19%, but 186,875 is 23.8% of 786,787 (editors' arithmetic); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: About 50% of current drinkers reported more than 100 g/week and 8.4% more than 350 g/week; median 96 g/week (5th to 95th percentiles 6 to 448). Intake was lower in more recent recruitment periods and weakly positively correlated with male sex, smoking, systolic blood pressure, HDL cholesterol, fibrinogen and lower socio-economic status.
key_findings.note: Table 1 counts give 8.7% above 350 g/week (52,429 of 599,912; editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Regression dilution ratio for alcohol 0.50 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.52) from 152,640 repeat assessments in 71,011 participants of 37 studies (median interval 5.6 years, 5th to 95th percentiles 1.04 to 13.5); those with repeat measures were younger, more often men and drank slightly more. All per-100 g/week HRs refer to long-term average (usual) intake estimated this way.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality rose with intake in a positive, curvilinear association, lowest for categories below 100 g/week, relative to current drinkers of >0 to ≤25 g/week (reference); similar in men and women, weaker at older ages. The aggregate of CVD outcomes showed a J-shaped association.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image and its category HRs were not extracted; the numbers are in appendix p 25 (not read). The threshold has no interval.

key_findings.finding: Per 100 g/week higher usual intake within current drinkers: stroke HR 1.14 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.17), coronary disease excluding MI 1.06 (1.00 to 1.11), heart failure 1.09 (1.03 to 1.15), fatal hypertensive disease 1.24 (1.15 to 1.33) and fatal aortic aneurysm 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28), roughly linear; MI 0.94 (0.91 to 0.97), approximately log-linear inverse. Adjusted for age, smoking and diabetes, stratified by sex and centre.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Abstract › Findings

key_findings.finding: In the subset with HDL cholesterol measured (61 cohorts, 9,911 MI events), adjustment for usual HDL cholesterol moved the MI HR per 100 g/week from 0.93 (0.88 to 0.97) to 1.00 (0.96 to 1.04) and strengthened coronary disease excluding MI from 1.07 (0.98 to 1.17) to 1.13 (1.05 to 1.22) and heart failure from 1.09 (1.00 to 1.19) to 1.14 (1.01 to 1.27). In the systolic blood pressure subset, adjustment weakened stroke from 1.16 (1.11 to 1.22) to 1.10 (1.06 to 1.14) and strengthened the inverse MI association from 0.95 (0.91 to 0.99) to 0.91 (0.87 to 0.94). Body-mass index changed little.

When never drinkers and former drinkers were included, the analysis reproduced the U-shaped associations with total CVD and all-cause mortality reported previously; never drinkers differed from current drinkers in sex, ethnicity, smoking and diabetes, which the authors take as supporting the restriction to current drinkers.
key_findings.note: Values only in the appendix (pp 12, 31; not read). This is the only place the study touches non-drinkers.

key_findings.finding: Results were described as similar with multiple imputation, fractional polynomials, fixed-effect pooling, inclusion of studies with fewer than five events, separate analyses of men and women, omission of the first 5 years of follow-up, exclusion of people with diabetes or other known chronic disease, and restriction to studies recording fatal and non-fatal events.
key_findings.note: No numbers in the main text (appendix pp 17, 18, 26, 32 to 37, not read).

key_findings.finding: Exploratory: at the same weekly amount, all-cause mortality associations were stronger in people drinking beer or spirits than wine and in those drinking on fewer days, including people drinking 100 g or more per occasion, but these groups smoked more and had other markers of lower socio-economic status; for CVD subtypes, beer and spirits HRs were not significantly higher than wine in direct comparisons.

Little heterogeneity between studies: I2 12% for stroke, 12% for MI, 26% for coronary disease excluding MI, 4% for heart failure, 33% for other CVD deaths. HRs for the CVD outcomes were broadly similar across regions, decades of enrolment, data sources and alcohol assessment methods, generally higher at younger ages, and did not vary substantially by sex, diabetes, lipids, body-mass index or smoking; no evidence of small-study effects or of non-proportional hazards.

Modelled life expectancy at age 40, compared with reported intake of >0 to ≤100 g/week (mean usual 56 g): about 6 months shorter for >100 to ≤200 g/week (mean usual 123 g), 1 to 2 years for >200 to ≤350 (208 g) and 4 to 5 years for >350 (367 g). Men above the UK limit of 112 g/week: 1.6 years shorter (1.3 to 1.8); above the US limit of 196 g/week: 2.7 years (2.4 to 3.1); women above 112 or 98 g/week: about 1.3 years (1.1 to 1.5). About 20% of the difference in men (slightly less in women) was attributed to CVD deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Model-based: HRs for baseline intake categories applied to US death rates for 2007 to 2010; reference is light drinkers, not non-drinkers.

key_findings.finding: The association of alcohol with cancers of the digestive system was confirmed and unchanged by further adjustment; adjustment for smoking amount abolished the apparent association with lung cancer.

The authors list as limitations: self-reported intake that is hard to harmonise; no measurement across the whole life course; outcome misclassification diluting associations; no access, in general, to non-fatal liver disease, injuries or psychiatric outcomes, so that benefits of lower intake were probably underestimated; and residual reverse causation from people who cut down because of illness, with some cohorts not recording other chronic disease; they call for randomized trials.

The published correction (Lancet 2018;391:2212, doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31168-1) corrects only the affiliation of one author (Makoto Daimon); no numbers were changed, so all values on this card are unaffected.
key_findings.locator: Department of Error notice, single paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 186,875 non-drinkers were 19% of 786,787 participants, but 186,875 is 23.8% of 786,787 (editors' arithmetic); 19% would fit a denominator of about 973,700.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of non-drinkers in the source cohorts cannot be stated from the article with certainty; quote counts, not the percentage.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives total participants of 356,819 (ERFC), 30,702 (EPIC-CVD) and 358,833 (UK Biobank), summing to 746,354, whereas the text starts from 786,787 participants with sufficient information (editors' arithmetic); the 40,433 difference is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The flow from eligible participants to the 599,912 analysed current drinkers cannot be reconstructed from the main text.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 8.4% drank more than 350 g/week, but the Table 1 counts for that category (25,432 + 1,796 + 25,201 = 52,429 of 599,912) give 8.7% (editors' arithmetic). Table 1 also labels the top category ≥350 g/week while the predefined categories are >250 to ≤350 and >350.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1; Methods › Study design, 3rd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 all-cause mortality events (32,813 + 784 + 6,720) sum to 40,317, against 40,310 deaths in the text and abstract (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the estimates; cite 40,310 as the authors' total.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 defines the CVD aggregate as MI, coronary heart disease and stroke, but the first-event counts for those outcomes sum to 34,619 (38,451 with heart failure and other CVD deaths), against 39,018 total CVD events (editors' arithmetic); the composition of the total is not stated in the main text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend
